extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (logic, metaphysics, epistemology)
extracted.subtask_description: A logical/epistemological taxonomy and account of what can be named or predicated (feelings, minds, bodies, attributes) and the grounds on which such predicates are justified. The text explains how sensations and states of consciousness ground our knowledge and the classification of qualities, relations, and quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge-of-objects-limited-to-sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: "all we know of objects is the sensations which they give us, and the order of the occurrence of those sensations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central epistemological claim: we can know only the sensations objects produce and the order in which they occur. Includes references to Berkeley and Kant (Noumenon vs. phenomenon) and the practical inevitability of attributing sensations to an external cause. Implication: claims about a thing 'in itself' (noumenon) are unknowable; focus inquiry on sensations/representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition-of-matter-as-substratum/external-cause
rubrics_metrics.description: "To this substratum the name Matter is usually given... the existence of matter can not be proved by extrinsic evidence... the belief is intuitive... mankind... refer their sensations to an external cause."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matter (body) is treated as the unknown external cause or substratum inferred from the ordered connexion of sensations. The text allows that existence of material substratum is not provable by extrinsic evidence and is commonly held as an intuitive necessity. Use this definition when speaking of 'body' in logical/epistemic analysis; avoid assuming we know its intrinsic nature beyond being the cause of sensations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition-of-mind-as-recipient/percipient
rubrics_metrics.description: "our conception of a mind is that of an unknown recipient or percipient"; "all which we are aware of, even in our own minds, is ... a certain 'thread of consciousness' ... a series of feelings."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mind is defined, analogously to body, as the unknown subject that feels and thinks; what we know of mind are only its states (sensations, thoughts, emotions, volitions). Any claim about the mind's 'innermost nature' beyond these states is unknowable within this framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes-grounded-on-sensations-(qualities)
rubrics_metrics.description: "the quality of whiteness ascribed to the object snow, is grounded on its exciting in us the sensation of white; ... the sensation is the only essential part of what is meant by the word; the only part which we ever can be concerned in proving."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualities (e.g., whiteness) are to be taken as grounded in the sensations objects excite. For logical purposes one may speak of 'qualities' but must recognize that proving a quality reduces to proving the corresponding sensation(s). The text contrasts this with the alternative view (qualities as powers inherent in objects) and recommends adopting language compatible with either view but emphasizes the sensation-grounding for logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tripartite-classification-of-attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: "Attributes are usually distributed under the three heads of Quality, Quantity, and Relation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A working taxonomy for attributes used throughout the analysis: treat attributes by whether they concern quality (sensible properties), quantity (extent/degree), or relation (involving other objects). This classification directs what kind of grounding (sensation, comparative sensation, joint facts) to seek when analysing predicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations-grounded-in-a-fundamentum_relationis
rubrics_metrics.description: "...in each of them there exists or occurs ... some fact or phenomenon, into which the two things which are said to be related to each other, both enter as parties concerned. This fact, or phenomenon, is what the Aristotelian logicians called the fundamentum relationis."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relations are to be analysed as grounded on some shared fact or phenomenon (fundamentum relationis) in which both relata partake (e.g., master/servant grounded on services performed; greater/less grounded on inclusion relations). When attributing a relation, identify the underlying fact-series of sensations or intentions that constitute it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple-relations-as-states-of-consciousness-(succession-simultaneity-likeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: "These, not being grounded on any fact or phenomenon distinct from the related objects themselves, do not admit of the same kind of analysis. But these relations, though not, like other relations, grounded on states of consciousness, are themselves states of consciousness: resemblance is nothing but our feeling of resemblance; succession is nothing but our feeling of succession."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat succession, simultaneity, likeness/unlikeness as primitive relations tied directly to states or feelings of consciousness. They resist reduction to an external fundamentum and must be recognized as basic faculties or presuppositions in any further analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resemblance-and-analogy-decomposed-into-component-likenesses
rubrics_metrics.description: "When we say of two things which consist of parts, that they are like one another, the likeness of the wholes does admit of analysis; it is compounded of likenesses between the various parts respectively, and of likeness in their arrangement."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex likenesses (e.g., portraits, mimicry) can be analyzed into multiple simpler resemblances among parts and arrangements. Analogy is resemblance of fundamenta relationis; when arguing analogy, specify which component resemblances are being relied upon to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity-grounded-on-differences-in-sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: "...when we say of two things that they differ in quantity ... the assertion is always grounded on a difference in the sensations which they excite."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences of quantity (more/less, greater/lesser) are to be understood as differences in the sensations they occasion (e.g., perceiving ten gallons vs one gallon). Use sensory-grounding when disputing or proving quantitative predicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes-of-minds-include-internal-states-and-effects-on-others
rubrics_metrics.description: "The attributes of minds, as well as those of bodies, are grounded on states of feeling or consciousness. ... attributes may also be ascribed to it ... grounded on the feelings which it excites in other minds. ... The word generosity ... expresses a certain state of mind, but ... also expresses that this state of mind excites in us another mental state, called approbation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing characteristics to minds, distinguish (a) the mind's habitual internal states (what the mind experiences) and (b) the effects those states have on other minds (social/praise-blame predicates). Some predicate-meanings are dual: descriptive of internal disposition and evaluative of others' responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding-occurrent-entity-redundancy-(qualities-as-reassertions)
rubrics_metrics.description: "When the physician stated that opium has a soporific virtue, he did not account for, but merely asserted over again, the fact that it produces sleep... In like manner, when we say that snow is white because it has the quality of whiteness, we are only re-asserting ... that it excites in us the sensation of white."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning against positing occult causes or redundant entities: saying an object 'has' a quality should not be treated as explaining the sensation beyond stating that the object produces that sensation. Logical analysis should avoid introducing unseen powers unless they add explanatory value beyond restating observable effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity-between-identity-and-undistinguishable-resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: "Resemblance, when it exists in the highest degree of all, amounting to undistinguishableness, is often called identity ... Great confusion of ideas is often produced ... by not being sufficiently alive to the fact ... that they use the same name to express ideas so different as those of identity and undistinguishable resemblance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful in terminology: reserve 'same' for strict identity and distinguish it from mere perfect resemblance or indistinguishability of appearances. Failing to make this distinction generates fallacies; clarify whether you mean numerical identity or phenomenal indistinguishability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final-classification-of-namable-things-(four-fold-list)
rubrics_metrics.description: "As the result, therefore, of our analysis, we obtain the following as an enumeration and classification of all Namable Things: 1st. Feelings, or States of Consciousness. 2d. The Minds which experience those feelings. 3d. The Bodies, or external objects which excite certain of those feelings, together with the powers or properties whereby they excite them. 4th, and last. The Successions and Co-existences, the Likenesses and Unlikenesses, between feelings or states of consciousness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the working taxonomy to be used in logical discourse: nameable things reduce to (1) feelings/states of consciousness, (2) minds, (3) bodies with their power-to-excite-sensations, and (4) relations among feelings (succession, coexistence, likeness). Use this four-fold scheme as the default classificatory apparatus in further logical analysis.
